scenario: AITA for catching my parents disputes on a video conference when I'm working from home? | I am in my early 20s and I have a full time job. I'm living at home right now because, right when cuarantine was starting, I tried to renew my apartment lease and my landlord refused me, saying he was selling the building for condos. So with all the shutdowns, I wasn't able to find a new apartment in time and my parents let me move back in. It's really not ideal and I've actually signed a new apartment lease that starts in a month. I wish it was sooner but housing near me is very competitive. My parents have always had a very disfunctional relationship. But they won't leave each other. No matter how much drama they have, I think they've lived like this too long to consider anything else. I have my work setup in the formal dining room which is rarely used. The room opens to the main entry hallway, and there is no door there. So there's less privacy than I'd prefer. I was hosting a meeting this morning and several of my coworkers were attending. They're all actually good friends of mine outside of work too; close enough friends that I've told them about my tumultuous childhood, my stresses moving back in with my family, etc. So when my parents came in the door in a full blown screaming match, in full view of the camera, I wasn't too shaken. First, unfortunately, that kind of thing has been really normalized for me, it doesn't register as a big deal. Second, it wasn't like the people in the meeting didn't already know my parents were high-tempered. So I just said "Hold on, can you still hear me? Not well? Sorry. Let's just take a coffee break then pick up from there." A couple people got up but my coworker Dan who's a good friend of mine stayed and asked me if I was all good. I said yeah, this shit was normal for all my life, I was just annoyed at the timing but I wasn't scared or some shit. My other co-workers trickled back in. My parents were still going hog wild in the hallway, and I eventually said "hey could yall keep it down, I'm presenting for a meeting." My dad saw that they were on camera first, and got really mad at me. Yelling at me to get the fuck out of his house. I went out to my car and took my laptop and finished the meeting in there. But when I came back in my parents were both over yelling at each other for the moment and they were both furious at me for "filming a private family matter for everyone to see" and shit like that. I said that I wasn't trying to film them, I was on camera myself because I was doing a presentation and they walked right in and started screaming. And if they'd stopped to think or look around at all they'd see I was trying to work quietly. My parents kicked me out and I'm at a hotel now. My parents want an apology and I don't know what to do. I think I might to keep the peace but I don't really feel bad for what I did. AITA for getting my parents argument on a video conference?

Okay, let's tackle this scenario. So the user is asking whether it's morally acceptable to have their parents' dispute caught on a video conference while working from home. The question is whether they're the asshole (AITA) for that.

First, I need to understand the situation. The person is in their early 20s, living with parents because they couldn't find a new apartment during quarantine. They have a new lease starting in a month. Their parents have a dysfunctional relationship, and they're used to the drama. They're working from home in the dining room, which has no door, so it's not private. During a work meeting with coworkers (who are also friends and know about their family situation), parents start arguing in the hallway, visible on camera. The person pauses the meeting, takes a coffee break, then when the parents keep yelling, asks them to keep it down. Dad sees himself on camera, gets mad, yells at them to get out of the house. The person leaves to finish the meeting in the car, then comes back to find parents furious, saying they filmed a private matter. The person says they weren't filming them intentionally, just working, and parents walked in. Parents kicked them out, want an apology.

Now, the question is whether the action (being on a work call where parents' argument was visible) is morally acceptable. The options are 1 for acceptable, 0 for not.

First, I need to consider the context. The person was working from home, in a space that's part of the house but not private (no door). They were hosting a work meeting with colleagues who already know about their family situation. The parents walked into the hallway during the meeting, which was visible on camera. The person didn't intentionally film them; it was a coincidence. They tried to handle it by pausing the meeting, then later asked parents to keep it down. The parents then got angry about being on camera, but the person wasn't recording them specifically—it was part of the work call.

Morally, the key points are: intentionality, privacy expectations, and responsibility. Did the person do something wrong by having the meeting in a space where parents could walk in? Well, the dining room is part of the house, and they have a right to work there. The parents entered the hallway, which is a common area. If the room has no door, then it's not a private space. So the parents walking in during a meeting isn't the person's fault. The person didn't set up to film them; it was accidental. The coworkers already knew about the family issues, so they weren't surprised. The person tried to manage the situation by pausing the meeting and asking parents to quiet down. The parents' reaction seems disproportionate—they're blaming the person for their own behavior (arguing in a shared space during a work call).

In terms of moral acceptability: the person wasn't intentionally exposing their parents. They were working, and the parents' argument happened to be on camera. The person didn't do anything wrong by having the meeting there. The parents should have been aware that the dining room is used for work, and if they were arguing, they should have considered the possibility of being heard or seen. Especially since the person had already asked them to keep it down. The parents' anger seems misplaced—they're the ones causing the disturbance in a shared space during a work meeting.

So the action (being on the call where parents' argument was visible) is morally acceptable. The person didn't do anything wrong. They were just working, and the parents walked in. The blame should be on the parents for arguing loudly in a place where someone is working, not on the person for having the meeting there.

Therefore, the answer should be 1 (morally acceptable). The excuse would explain that the person was working in a common area, didn't intentionally film the parents, and the parents' behavior was the issue, not the person's actions.
